evidence: Cic. Sen. 49: dēfectiōnēs sōlis et lūnae multō ante nōbīs praedīcere
terms.comment: Not to be confused with praedicō, praedicāre (first conjugation), to proclaim, to praise (Lewis & Short). The noun is praedictiō, a prediction (Cic. Div. 2.54).
To sense what is coming rather than to work it out (Cicero’s definition: futūra ante sentīre).

evidence: Cic. Att. 6.9.5: dē rē pūblicā, quam praevideō in summīs perīculīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To see beforehand, in the mind. For guessing what is coming see guess (dīvīnāre).

phrases.latin: quam dēlectābat eum dēfectiōnēs sōlis et lūnae multō ante nōbīs praedīcere!
phrases.english: how he loved to predict eclipses of the sun and moon for us long before!

phrases.latin: is igitur, quī ante sāgit quam oblāta rēs est, dīcitur praesāgīre, id est futūra ante sentīre
phrases.english: so the one who perceives keenly before the thing has appeared is said to have a presentiment, that is, to feel the future beforehand

sources: Lewis & Short: praedico · Lewis & Short: praedictio · Lewis & Short: praesagio · Lewis & Short: praevideo
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
